title: Tacos, Tones, and Technology
summary: An Evening with Clinton Township Fire-Rescue-EMS Station 4 I recently had the opportunity to spend an evening with the firefighters and paramedics at Station 4 in Clinton Township, Michigan. It was an unforgettable experience, one that combined candid conversations, hands-on learning, and a deep appreciation for the people who answer the call when the rest of us need help most. On any given day, or night, these crews respond to everything from structure fires to medical emergencies to...
body_text: Tacos, Tones, and Technology August 11, 2026 by Brian Heath An Evening with Clinton Township Fire-Rescue-EMS Station 4 I recently had the opportunity to spend an evening with the firefighters and paramedics at Station 4 in Clinton Township, Michigan. It was an unforgettable experience, one that combined candid conversations, hands-on learning, and a deep appreciation for the people who answer the call when the rest of us need help most. On any given day, or night, these crews respond to everything from structure fires to medical emergencies to false alarms. It’s a profession defined by unpredictability, urgency, and an unwavering commitment to service. Inside the Station The visit began with a tour of the station: the engine bay with its organized and meticulously maintained space, the administrative workspace, the dorms where crews catch what sleep they can, and the shared living area where they spend much of their downtime together. One of the most fascinating pieces of equipment I saw was the LUCAS automated CPR device, a machine that delivers consistent, precise chest compressions during cardiac arrest. While the device works tirelessly, paramedics are freed up to focus on other lifesaving interventions such as airway management and IV access. It was just one example of how technology is augmenting, not replacing, the expertise and coordination of these professionals. I also gained insight into the different roles within the department and how each team member relies on technology differently. Whether it’s the lieutenant coordinating response strategy, the firefighter navigating hazardous environments, or the paramedic delivering critical care, their tools are tailored to help them act quickly, decisively, and safely. Tacos and Real Conversations After the tour, I joined the crew for dinner in the station’s main gathering area. On the menu: tacos prepared by the team. It was relaxed, genuine, and exactly what you’d expect from a group that operates like a second family. Over dinner, the conversation turned to the realities of the job. We talked about the high volume of non-emergency 911 calls, which continue to strain resources and limit availability for true emergencies. We discussed the long-term health risks firefighters face, particularly elevated cancer rates tied to exposure to toxins and carcinogens at fire scenes. And we talked about the tones , the piercing alarms that can go off at any moment, day or night, jolting crews from sleep into immediate action. It’s hard to imagine being awakened by bright lights and loud tones and, within seconds, needing to absorb critical dispatch information, gear up, and head out the door. But for them, it’s routine. When the Tones Drop And then, right on cue, it happened. About halfway through dinner, the tones rang out. A dispatcher’s voice filled the station, describing the call. At the same time, that same information was instantly pushed to mobile devices, phones and tablets carried by the team. Within moments, dinner was paused and we were headed out. This is where Tyler’s technology in action, supporting first responders in real time, under real pressure. As we responded to calls, I watched how dispatch data flowed seamlessly into the hands of the crew: Real-time call notes from 911 dispatch Turn-by-turn navigation and mapping GIS overlays showing building layouts, hydrant locations, and other critical information Pre-incident planning data, including access points and hazards Even on calls that ultimately turned out to be false alarms, the importance of this information was clear. Seconds matter. Having accurate, consolidated data, accessible in a single interface, helps teams respond faster, make better decisions, and operate more safely. Tyler’s platform brings together dispatch, GIS, records, and inspection data into one unified experience, ensuring that from the moment a call is received to the final report, responders have the information they need. A Real Call, Real Impact Later in the evening, around 10:00 PM, we responded to a medical call that required patient transport. Firefighters/paramedics and an ambulance crew worked side by side, assessing the patient, gathering medical history, stabilizing conditions, and preparing for transport. Again, technology was present at every step: Capturing patient information on scene Coordinating across agencies Supporting documentation and reporting After returning to the station, the crew still had work to do. Reports needed to be completed, including detailed documentation of the incident, patient condition, and care provided. Even with modern tools, this process takes time and precision. Explore Tyler’s Fire & EMS Suite From prevention and preparedness to reporting and administration, Tyler’s Fire & EMS suite offers innovative tools to support public safety needs at every level. From Dispatch to Disposition After nearly five hours, my visit came to an end. For the crew, it was just another stretch of a 24-hour shift, with more calls likely ahead before morning. Personally, the experience left me with a deep appreciation for the people behind the profession: their bravery, resilience, teamwork, and quiet dedication to serving others in moments of crisis. Professionally, it reinforced something I’m incredibly proud of. At Tyler, we often talk about supporting the public safety ecosystem, from dispatch to disposition. Seeing that come to life inside Station 4 was powerful. It’s not just software; it’s a critical layer of support that helps first responders do their jobs more effectively, improves outcomes for the communities they serve, and ultimately helps save lives. Final Thoughts Tacos, tones, and technology. It’s a simple phrase, but it captures the essence of that evening: The human connection around the dinner table The relentless urgency of the tones And the technology quietly working in the background to tie it all together We all hope we never need to call 911. But if we do, it’s reassuring to know that behind that call is a team of highly trained professionals, equipped with both the courage and the tools to respond when it matters most. And when they help us get home safely to our families, it means everything to know we’re helping them do the same. Related Content × Your message has been sent!

title: Best online homeschool curriculum programs: how to choose the right fit
summary: Compare the top online homeschool curriculum programs for 2026. Full-curriculum vs. a-la-carte, cost breakdown, ESA compatibility, and honest watch-fors to help you choose.
body_text: What "curriculum" means in the homeschool world (and why the word is slippery) When a parent searches "homeschool curriculum online," they could mean at least three different things: a full-year, all-subjects program that replaces a traditional school (think K12 or Connections Academy); a subject-specific set of textbooks and lessons they teach themselves (think Saxon Math or All About Reading); or a collection of live, teacher-led classes they assemble from multiple sources. Each model works. None of them is the "best" in every situation. The right choice depends on how much structure your family needs, whether you want live instruction or self-paced materials, how much you want to teach yourself versus outsource, and what your state requires. This guide compares the major online curriculum options across those dimensions so you can make the decision with real information instead of marketing copy. Full-curriculum programs: all-in-one, structured, ready to go These programs provide a complete K-12 (or near-complete) curriculum across all core subjects. You enroll, and the platform handles scope, sequence, lesson delivery, and often grading. They're the closest thing to "school at home" without a traditional school. Time4Learning Self-paced, multimedia lessons covering math, language arts, science, and social studies for PreK-12. Parents set the schedule; the platform delivers the content and auto-grades most assignments. Cost: ~$35/month (PreK-8), ~$40/month (9-12) Instruction model: Self-paced, animated/interactive lessons. No live teacher. Best for: Families who want an affordable, structured curriculum they can run independently. Watch for: No live teacher interaction. The social component is entirely on you. Writing feedback is limited to automated grading. Power Homeschool (Acellus) Video-based, self-paced curriculum with over 500 courses. Acellus provides the instruction platform; Power Homeschool is the parent-facing portal. Includes science virtual labs and automated diagnostics. Cost: ~$25/month per student Instruction model: Pre-recorded video lessons with embedded quizzes. No live interaction. Best for: Budget-conscious families who want a structured, video-driven approach. Watch for: Limited parent customization. The curriculum follows a fixed sequence, which can feel rigid if your child is ahead or behind in specific subjects. K12 (Stride) K12 operates as a tuition-free virtual public school in many states, meaning your child is technically enrolled in a public school and follows its calendar, testing schedule, and attendance requirements. They also offer a private, tuition-based option (K12 Private Academy) for families who want the curriculum without the public school requirements. Cost: Free (public school option, state-dependent) or ~$5,000-$8,000/year (private academy) Instruction model: Mix of live online classes and self-paced work, depending on grade and state. Best for: Families who want a free, structured, accredited option with some live instruction and don't mind following a school calendar. Watch for: The free option is a virtual public school, not homeschooling. You follow their schedule, take their tests, and your child is enrolled in the public school system. In some states, this means you lose homeschool status. Flexibility is limited. Connections Academy Similar to K12's public-school model: tuition-free virtual public school with a full curriculum, live classes, and certified teachers. Available in roughly 30 states. Cost: Free (public school enrollment) Instruction model: Live and recorded lessons, certified teachers, school-issued materials. Best for: Families who want a full school experience at home with no cost. Watch for: Same trade-off as K12's free tier. This is virtual public school, not homeschool. State availability varies, and you follow their academic calendar. Withdrawing mid-year can be complicated. BJU Press and Abeka Comprehensive, faith-based curricula with daily lesson plans covering all core subjects plus Bible. BJU Press leans academic with critical-thinking emphasis; Abeka follows a more traditional, drill-based approach. Both offer video instruction options. Cost: $500-$1,200/year depending on grade and format (textbook vs. video) Instruction model: Textbook-based with optional video lessons. Parent-taught or video-taught. Best for: Families who want a faith-integrated, structured curriculum with clear daily lesson plans. Watch for: Worldview alignment is strong and specific. If you're looking for secular or worldview-neutral content, these aren't it. Curriculum is also fairly rigid, with less room for child-led exploration. A-la-carte and supplemental platforms: build your own These platforms don't try to be everything. Instead, they let you pick the specific subjects, skill levels, and formats your child needs. You're the curriculum architect; they provide the building materials. Outschool Live, teacher-led online classes across 140,000+ topics, from algebra tutoring to creative writing workshops to AP exam prep. Classes are taught by vetted teachers in small groups (averaging 3-4 kids) or 1:1. You pick the classes; there's no fixed sequence or enrollment window. Cost: Per-class pricing, typically $10-$25/class. No subscription. Instruction model: Live video classes with real teachers, real-time interaction, and feedback. Best for: Families who want to assemble a custom curriculum from live instruction, fill gaps in another program, or add enrichment and socialization. Also strong for families using ESA funds , since Outschool is an approved provider on Odyssey, ClassWallet, and other state ESA platforms. Watch for: Outschool is not a packaged curriculum. If you want someone else to handle scope and sequence across all subjects, you'll need to pair it with a core program or build your own plan. Our step-by-step curriculum-building guide walks through how to do that. Khan Academy Free, self-paced lessons and practice across math, science, computing, history, and test prep. Khanmigo (AI tutor) adds a conversational layer for $44/year. Cost: Free (core platform). Khanmigo: $44/year. Instruction model: Pre-recorded video lessons with adaptive practice exercises. No live instruction. Best for: Supplementing math and science. The mastery-based progression is genuinely useful for filling gaps. Watch for: No live teacher, no writing instruction, and limited humanities content. It's a supplement, not a standalone curriculum. IXL Adaptive, skill-based practice platform covering math, language arts, science, and social studies for K-12. Provides diagnostic assessments and skill plans. Cost: ~$10-$20/month per subject Instruction model: Practice problems with immediate feedback. No teaching, just practice. Best for: Drill and reinforcement after you've taught a concept. Diagnostics are useful for identifying gaps. Watch for: IXL is practice, not instruction. It doesn't teach concepts. A child who doesn't understand fractions won't learn them from IXL alone.

title: Are Male Fertility Tests & Supplements HSA/FSA Eligible?
summary: At-home sperm tests often clear at checkout, while fertility supplements need a Letter of Medical Necessity. See what qualifies and how to pay with Flex.
body_text: Male factor contributes to a substantial share of infertility cases, and yet the testing and treatment side of that equation gets a fraction of the attention. If you and your partner are trying to conceive, a sperm test is a low-friction place to start, and for qualifying customers, your HSA or FSA can go toward it, along with the supplements a clinician may recommend afterwards. Here is what this guide covers: Is male fertility testing and treatment HSA and FSA eligible? Why at-home tests and monitors are treated differently from supplements at checkout. Types of medical conditions that qualify male fertility products to be HSA and FSA eligible. The diagnoses that support a Letter of Medical Necessity. How to buy male fertility products using your HSA or FSA directly or through reimbursement. Both routes, with the documentation each one needs. 4 male fertility products you can shop with Flex. Tests, monitors, and supplements from brands in the Flex marketplace. The split between tests and supplements drives almost everything else in this guide, so that is where we'll start. Is male fertility testing and treatment HSA and FSA eligible? For qualifying customers, yes, and the practical answer depends on which kind of product you are buying. At-home sperm tests and fertility monitors generally clear on their own. A semen analysis kit is a diagnostic test. Nothing about it has a plausible non-medical use, so it carries its purpose on its face. Products in this group are typically classified for auto-substantiation, which means the transaction goes through when you pay with your HSA or FSA card, with no letter, no consultation, and no form to submit afterwards. Fertility supplements generally require a Letter of Medical Necessity. A capsule containing CoQ10, zinc, or omega-3s looks identical whether it is being taken to support sperm motility under a clinician's guidance or as a general daily vitamin. That ambiguity is what makes supplements dual-purpose products, and it is why a clinician has to connect the product to a diagnosed condition before an administrator will treat the expense as medical care. Section 213(d) of the Internal Revenue Code defines medical care as amounts paid for "the diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment, or prevention of disease, or for the purpose of affecting any structure or function of the body." Male factor infertility is a diagnosable medical condition, and both testing for it and supporting its treatment can fall within that definition. What differs between a test and a supplement is not whether the statute reaches it, but how much documentation an administrator needs in order to see the medical purpose. Two terms worth keeping separate, because people conflate them constantly. Substantiation is what happens at the moment you pay. Certain products are flagged in merchant systems so the card transaction clears automatically. It is a payment-processing step running on merchant inventory data, not a ruling from the IRS. Eligibility is what your plan administrator concludes if the expense is ever reviewed. Your administrator always has the final say. An expense later determined to be non-qualified becomes taxable income, generally with an additional 20% tax in the case of an HSA, though some exceptions apply. That is why keeping your receipt matters even on a purchase that cleared without friction. One more thing worth knowing: classification is resolved per product , not per brand. The same company can sell a test that auto-substantiates and a supplement that requires a letter, which is the case for at least one brand in the Flex marketplace. Flex shows the current classification for an item at checkout, and classification can change, so treat the product page as the source. Do you always need a Letter of Medical Necessity to buy male fertility products with your HSA/FSA? No, and knowing which side of the line a product sits on saves you a step. A Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN) is a short note from a licensed clinician confirming that a product supports treatment or mitigation of a diagnosed condition. You will generally not need one for at-home semen analysis and sperm test kits, or for fertility and hormone monitors including male fertility testing kits. These are diagnostics, and they typically substantiate on their own. You generally will need one for male fertility supplements, including motility and sperm-quality formulations. Where a supplement is classified that way, the product page will say so before you pay. Because classification is set per item, check the page rather than assuming a whole category behaves one way. If a product needs a letter, Flex connects you asynchronously with a licensed clinician in your state, who reviews your consultation and decides whether to issue it. There is no appointment to book and no waiting room. For a qualifying customer, an LMN is usually all it takes, though whether a letter is issued is always the clinician's medical judgment rather than a foregone conclusion, and your plan administrator still makes the final call on the expense. A useful sequence: test first, supplement second. A semen analysis usually clears without documentation, and the results are what a clinician will want to see anyway when assessing whether a supplement regimen is warranted. Types of medical conditions that qualify male fertility products to be HSA and FSA eligible Where a Letter of Medical Necessity is required, it has to connect the product to a diagnosed condition. These are the diagnoses that most commonly support male fertility products: Male factor infertility. The umbrella diagnosis, applied when testing identifies a male contribution to a couple's difficulty conceiving. It is the most direct basis for a letter covering a fertility supplement, and it is typically established through semen analysis rather than assumed. Abnormal spermatozoa. Findings of atypical sperm morphology, meaning the shape and structure of the cells, identified on a semen analysis. Morphology is one of the standard parameters a lab reports, alongside count and motility. Reduced sperm motility. Sperm that do not move effectively have difficulty reaching and fertilizing an egg, regardless of how many are present. Motility is a parameter many fertility supplement formulations are aimed at, which is why it often appears as the documented basis for one. Azoospermia and arrest of spermatogenesis. The absence of measurable sperm in the ejaculate, or a halt in sperm production at some stage of development. These are significant clinical findings that warrant a specialist workup, and any product recommendation would sit inside a broader treatment plan. Unexplained infertility. Where a couple has been trying to conceive without success and standard testing has not identified a cause. A clinician may still connect a product to it, though administrators vary in how they treat this. Hormonal imbalance. Testosterone, FSH, and LH levels outside expected ranges are associated with changes in sperm production. Where bloodwork documents an imbalance, the connection between treatment and reproductive function is easier to establish. Obesity as it relates to fertility. Elevated BMI is associated with changes in hormone levels and sperm parameters, and clinicians managing fertility often address it as part of the plan. Where a clinician documents that link, it can support the specific product the clinician names. Two things to be realistic about. First, these are conditions a clinician diagnoses; a self-assessment that something feels off is not the same thing, which is part of why testing comes first. Second, buying a supplement as general wellness support, with no diagnosis and no clinician involvement, is the case an administrator is least likely to treat as medical care. That is what dual-purpose means in practice: the everyday use is a personal expense, and a documented medical need is what changes the treatment. How to buy male fertility products using your HSA or FSA directly or through reimbursement Two routes. Paying directly is faster and involves no forms; reimbursement is the fallback when you have already paid out of pocket. 1. Pay with your HSA/FSA directly at checkout Choose your product from a store that offers Flex at checkout. The brands in the next section are all in the Flex marketplace. Check the eligibility shown on the product page. It tells you whether the item substantiates automatically or requires a Letter of Medical Necessity, which is the difference between a two-minute checkout and one that includes a short consultation. For a test or monitor, pay with your HSA or FSA card. For products classified for auto-substantiation, the transaction clears without further steps. For a supplement, complete the short consultation. You answer a few questions about your health and any testing you have had. A licensed clinician in your state reviews your responses and, if they agree your condition warrants it, issues the Letter of Medical Necessity. It happens in the same checkout flow rather than as a separate appointment. Review times vary, and the decision is the clinician's. Keep your records. Flex stores your receipt, and your LMN where one was issued, so both are in one place if your administrator asks. Letters commonly specify a duration, which matters for a supplement you plan to reorder. 2. Make a reimbursement claim If you have already bought a test or a supplement with a personal card, you can ask your administrator to reimburse you. Find an itemized receipt showing the merchant, date, item, and amount. A card statement line alone is usually not enough. Check the timing rules before you file. FSA expenses generally must be incurred during the plan year they are claimed against. HSA expenses must be incurred after your HSA was established, so a purchase predating the account cannot be reimbursed from it. Understand how letters obtained after the fact are treated. Many administrators require the LMN to be dated so that it covers the period when the expense was incurred. A letter obtained months later to justify an earlier purchase may not be accepted, so confirm with your administrator rather than assuming. Obtain the Letter of Medical Necessity if the product needs one and you do not already have one covering the purchase. Submit the claim through your administrator's portal or app, attaching the receipt and any supporting documentation. Wait for the determination. Approval is not automatic. If approved, funds usually arrive by direct deposit or check. Because supplement regimens typically run for several months and get reordered, paying directly is worth setting up properly the first time rather than filing a claim every cycle. 4 male fertility products you can shop with Flex These brands are in the Flex marketplace, so you can shop them and pay with your HSA or FSA card. Eligibility is shown per product at checkout, and it is worth checking, since a brand can sell products on both sides of the line. Product Brand What it does At Home Sperm Test for Male Fertility SWMR Fertility An at-home semen analysis for men who want a baseline before involving a clinic. Classified for auto-substantiation, so it typically clears at checkout without a letter. Mira Male Fertility Kit Mira Part of Mira's at-home hormone and fertility testing system, which also covers ovulation and cycle tracking for a partner. Classified for auto-substantiation. ConceptionXR® Motility Support For Men Theralogix A physician-formulated supplement aimed at sperm motility and reproductive health. Classified as requiring a Letter of Medical Necessity. Male Fertility Supplement SWIMCLUB A capsule and omega-3 softgel regimen formulated to support sperm count, motility, and quality. Classified as requiring a Letter of Medical Necessity. Check each product page for current specifications, which vary by product and change over time. Other brands in the Flex marketplace also carry products classified for male fertility support, including VB Health , Xendurance , and Mars GHC . On the female and couples side, the marketplace includes Theralogix, Osh Wellness , Happy V , Good Clean Love , and emilia george , alongside cycle and ovulation tracking from kegg , Tempdrop , and OvuSense . Eligibility for each is shown on the product page. Start with a test, then talk to a clinician If you are early in this process, an at-home sperm test is a low-friction first step, and it usually needs nothing beyond your HSA or FSA card at checkout. If testing points toward a supplement regimen, Flex connects you asynchronously with a licensed clinician in your state who can assess whether to issue a Letter of Medical Necessity, in the same flow, with no appointment to book. Keep reading: Using Your HSA/FSA for Fertility Treatments & Devices · What is a Letter of Medical Necessity? · What makes a product or service an IRS qualified HSA/FSA expense Eligibility may vary by plan and administrator, and not all products or customers qualify. Product classification is determined per item and can change, so the eligibility shown at checkout governs. Where a Letter of Medical Necessity is required, whether a letter is issued is determined by the licensed clinician based on your consultation. This is general information, not tax, legal, or medical advice. Consult your plan administrator or tax advisor.

title: Best MCP Servers for Developers [2026]
summary: The MCP servers worth running in 2026, organized by job, labelled by who maintains them, with the security trade-off stated instead of buried.
body_text: Most developers need six MCP servers, not fifty: a filesystem server, Git, GitHub, one database server in read-only mode, Playwright for browsers, and something that supplies current documentation. Everything after that is situational. This guide sorts MCP servers by the job they do rather than by vendor logo, and it says who maintains each one. That last part matters more than it sounds. Many servers still recommended by name in "top MCP servers" lists were archived in 2025 and now sit in a repository whose README states, in capitals, that no security guarantees are provided for them. If a list still tells you to install the reference PostgreSQL or GitHub server, it was written from memory rather than from the repository. What Is an MCP Server? An MCP server is a small program that exposes tools and data to an AI agent through the Model Context Protocol. Your agent calls those tools instead of you copying output between windows. It solves a boring but expensive problem. Before MCP, every agent needed a bespoke integration for every tool. Now one server works with every client that speaks the protocol, including Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor. The specification defines exactly two standard transports: stdio for servers that run as a local process, and Streamable HTTP for servers you connect to at a URL. The older HTTP plus SSE transport is formally deprecated , so a setup guide telling you to add a server with --transport sse is out of date. The split you care about is local versus remote . A local server runs on your machine, sees your files, and needs installing. A remote server is a hosted URL behind OAuth, and needs nothing installed. Remote has become the default for anything a company runs itself. If you want to understand the protocol rather than pick servers off a shelf, our roundup of MCP tutorials and courses is the companion piece. This article is about what to run. Official, Vendor-Built, or Community: How to Read Any MCP Server List Every MCP server falls into one of three maintenance tiers, and the tier predicts reliability better than the star count. Tier Who maintains it What that gets you Example Reference server The MCP project itself Small, simple, tracks the spec, no product behind it Filesystem, Git, Memory Vendor-built The company whose product it wraps Ships with the product, first to new features, usually OAuth GitHub, Linear, Supabase Community Someone who does not own the product Often the only option, quality varies, read the source Postgres MCP Pro The reference servers are what people mean by "official," and there are currently seven: Everything, Fetch, Filesystem, Git, Memory, Sequential Thinking, and Time. Thirteen others were retired to a separate archive repository , including the GitHub, GitLab, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Slack, Sentry, Google Drive, Puppeteer, and Brave Search servers. Only two of those entries carry a redirect to a successor, and in Slack's case the README is already behind reality, because Slack has since shipped a server of its own. Treat the archive as a list of things to replace, not as a directory. There is also an official registry , still labelled preview rather than generally available. It gives you provenance, since reverse-DNS namespaces are tied to a verified GitHub account or domain. It does not vet code. The registry's own documentation says it delegates security scanning to the underlying package registries. Before installing anything, run four checks: Who maintains it. Vendor-built beats community for anything touching production. When it last shipped. The protocol changed materially in 2026, and a server untouched for a year may not speak the current transport. What access it asks for. A token scoped to every repository you can see is very different from one scoped to a single repository. Whether it has a read-only mode. If it does, start there. The Best MCP Servers by Job Files Filesystem is the reference server for reading, writing, moving, and searching files inside directories you explicitly allow, published as @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem . Most agents already have file access built in, so the real use case is giving one scoped access to a directory outside your project, such as a notes folder or a design export. Git, GitHub, and GitLab Git is the reference server for local repository work: status, diffs, log, branches, commits, published to PyPI as mcp-server-git . It works on any repository on disk, with no account involved. The GitHub MCP server is GitHub's own, and it is the most useful single server on this list. It covers issues, pull requests, code search, Actions, and releases, as a local install or a hosted endpoint. Two features deserve deliberate use: read-only mode, which disables every write tool regardless of configuration, and toolsets, which expose only the parts you use. GitLab publishes its own server per instance. Databases The reference PostgreSQL and SQLite servers are both archived. For Postgres, the widely used replacement is Postgres MCP Pro , a third-party server with a restricted access mode that limits the agent to read-only transactions, plus index tuning and health checks that go beyond running queries. SQLite has no vendor successor at all; multi-database servers such as DBHub are the practical route. If your database is hosted, prefer the vendor's server. Supabase ships one with read-only and project-scoped modes, and its own security guidance is blunt about the boundary: never connect AI agents directly to production data. Browser automation and testing Playwright MCP is Microsoft's, and it is the strongest server in this category. Rather than feeding the model screenshots, it drives pages through Playwright's accessibility tree, so the agent works from structured element roles and text instead of pixels. That makes it deterministic in a way vision-based automation is not, though the package is still pre-1.0. Chrome DevTools MCP is the Chrome team's, and it answers a different question. It records performance traces, lists network requests, and reads console messages from a live browser, which turns "the page feels slow" into something an agent can investigate. Search, fetch, and live documentation Fetch is the reference server that retrieves a web page and converts it to markdown, published as mcp-server-fetch , and it respects robots.txt by default. For search proper, Brave, Exa, Tavily, and Perplexity all maintain their own servers, most of which want an API key. Context7 from Upstash solves the problem where your agent confidently writes code against a library version that shipped two years ago. It pulls version-specific documentation on demand, locally or hosted. Team tools The pattern here is uniform: the vendor hosts it, OAuth handles the login, nothing is installed. Linear runs one at https://mcp.linear.app/mcp covering issues, projects, and comments, with a separate read-only URL if you want the agent to look without touching. Notion , Sentry , Atlassian , and Stripe publish hosted endpoints too, and Sentry's is the example Anthropic uses for connecting an OAuth server. Slack now runs an official server as well, after a long stretch where community forks were the only option. There is no good reason to run a local process to read your own issue tracker. Cloud and deployment Cloudflare runs a catalog of managed remote servers split by product area, all OAuth-secured. AWS, Azure, Vercel, and Netlify each followed some version of the same pattern. The rule of thumb: if the vendor publishes a hosted MCP endpoint, use it rather than a community wrapper around their REST API. Memory and context Memory is the reference server that maintains a local knowledge graph across conversations, and Sequential Thinking exposes one tool that lets a model work through a problem in revisable steps. Both are small, both are useful, and both get installed and then quietly forgotten. Explanation and codebase walkthroughs This category answers "explain this to me" rather than "do this for me," and it is newer than the rest. DeepWiki , from the team behind Devin, is a free remote server with no authentication that lets an agent read generated documentation for a public GitHub repository and ask questions about it. The limit is public repositories only. Scrimba Explain works against your own code instead. It is an MCP plugin at https://scrimba.com/explain/mcp that runs with Claude Code, Codex and ChatGPT, and any MCP-capable agent. You ask a question about your codebase, your agent researches it using the context it already has, and what comes back is a narrated video walkthrough rather than a wall of text. It is free during open beta, and like any AI tool it can be wrong, so check anything important. Job Server Maintainer Local or remote Files Filesystem Reference Local Repositories GitHub MCP server Vendor Both Local Git Git Reference Local Postgres Postgres MCP Pro Community Local Browsers Playwright MCP Vendor Local Web performance Chrome DevTools MCP Vendor Local Library docs Context7 Vendor Both Issue tracking Linear Vendor Remote Public repo Q&A DeepWiki Vendor Remote Codebase walkthroughs Scrimba Explain Vendor Remote What MCP Servers Actually Cost You in Security An MCP server runs with whatever access you grant it, and the model decides when to use it. Those two facts together are the entire security story. The mechanism worth understanding is prompt injection through tool results . Your agent reads whatever a tool returns, and it cannot reliably tell data from instructions. A bug report, a web page, or a support ticket can contain text written to look like a command. Simon Willison calls the dangerous combination the lethal trifecta : access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally. Connect enough servers and you assemble all three without deciding to. This is not theoretical. Invariant Labs demonstrated an attack where a malicious issue filed on a public repository coerced an agent into reading private repositories and publishing the contents in a public pull request. Their conclusion is the uncomfortable part: it was not a bug in the server's code. The specification is candid about where the guarantees stop: MCP itself cannot enforce these security principles at the protocol level. Anthropic says something similar, noting that it reviews connectors against listing criteria but does not security-audit or manage any MCP server . What you get instead are controls that shrink the blast radius: Use read-only mode wherever a server offers one. GitHub, Linear, Supabase, and Postgres MCP Pro all have one. Scope tokens narrowly. One repository, one project, one database, not everything the token can reach. Keep production data out of it. Point servers at staging. Let your client ask. Permission prompts exist for this, and switching them off is the fastest way to lose the protection. Prefer servers you can read. For community servers, the source is the audit. None of this is a reason to avoid MCP. It is a reason to run six servers you understand rather than thirty you collected. How Do You Add an MCP Server? Adding an MCP server takes one command in most clients. In Claude Code, a remote server is claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url> , and a local one is claude mcp add <name> -- npx -y <package> . Servers install at three scopes: local to you, project (written to .mcp.json and shared through git), or user across all your projects. Run /mcp to check status and handle any OAuth login. The official documentation has the details, and our guide to using Claude Code covers where MCP fits in the workflow. Other clients differ in syntax, not concept, and Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor all run the same servers. How Many MCP Servers Should You Actually Run? Fewer than you think. Every connected server loads its tool definitions into the model's context before you type anything, so each one costs tokens and makes tool selection harder. Anthropic's engineering team put numbers on the problem : rewriting one multi-tool workflow so results stopped passing through the model dropped it from roughly 150,000 tokens to 2,000. Connected surface area is not free. Sensible starting points: Learning to code: none. Get comfortable directing an agent first, and our guide to agentic coding is a better next step than any server. Building side projects: GitHub in read-only mode, plus Context7. Working on a team: add your issue tracker, a scoped database server, and Playwright if you own tests. Add the fourth when you have felt the absence of it, not before. Frequently Asked Questions What are MCP servers used for? MCP servers give an AI agent controlled access to real systems: your files, repositories, databases, browser, issue tracker, and documentation. Instead of pasting output into a chat window, the agent calls a tool directly, reads the result, and continues working. Are MCP servers free? Most are open source and free to run. The reference servers, Playwright, Chrome DevTools, and Context7 all cost nothing. What you may pay for is the underlying service, since a hosted server still requires an account, and several search servers need a paid API key. Which MCP servers work with Claude Code? All of them. MCP is a shared protocol, so any server works with any compliant client, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Claude Desktop. The differences are in setup syntax and how each client handles permissions, not in which servers are compatible. Are MCP servers safe to use? They are as safe as the access you grant them. The specification states plainly that it cannot enforce security at the protocol level, so the real controls are read-only modes, narrowly scoped tokens, keeping production data out, and leaving your client's permission prompts switched on. Which MCP server can explain a codebase to me? DeepWiki answers questions about public GitHub repositories through generated documentation. For your own code, Scrimba Explain returns a narrated video walkthrough of whatever you asked about, using the context your agent already has. Both sit alongside Context7, which supplies current library documentation rather than explanations. Key Takeaways Six servers cover most developers: Filesystem, Git, GitHub, a read-only database server, Playwright, and Context7. Thirteen reference servers were archived in 2025, including GitHub, PostgreSQL, SQLite, and Slack, and the archive states that no security guarantees are provided for them. Seven remain active: Everything, Fetch, Filesystem, Git, Memory, Sequential Thinking, and Time. The official MCP registry is still in preview and gives you provenance, not a security audit. An MCP server runs with whatever access you grant it, and prompt injection through tool results is a real attack, not a hypothetical one. Read-only modes, narrow tokens, and staging data are the mitigations that exist today and cost nothing to use. Every connected server spends context before you type, so a small deliberate set beats a large collected one. To build a server rather than install one, Scrimba's Intro to Model Context Protocol spends 37 minutes registering tools and resources on a Weather server in Node.js, and the AI Engineer Path places MCP alongside embeddings, agents, and context engineering. Both sit on the Pro plan at $24.50 per month billed annually, discounts are available, and Scrimba's free courses include completion certificates. Sources Model Context Protocol, accessed August 2026: Reference servers: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers Archived servers: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers-archived Transports: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports Deprecations: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/deprecated Security best practices: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/security_best_practices Registry: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/registry/about Vendors and research, accessed August 2026: Anthropic, Claude Code security: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/security Anthropic, MCP in Claude Code: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp Anthropic, code execution with MCP: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/code-execution-with-mcp GitHub MCP Server: https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server Playwright MCP: https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp Chrome DevTools MCP: https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp Postgres MCP Pro: https://github.com/crystaldba/postgres-mcp DBHub: https://github.com/bytebase/dbhub Supabase, defense in depth for MCP: https://supabase.com/blog/defense-in-depth-mcp Context7: https://github.com/upstash/context7 Cloudflare MCP servers: https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/model-context-protocol/cloudflare/servers-for-cloudflare/ Linear MCP server: https://linear.app/docs/mcp Slack MCP server: https://docs.slack.dev/ai/slack-mcp-server/ DeepWiki MCP: https://docs.devin.ai/work-with-devin/deepwiki-mcp Invariant Labs, GitHub MCP exploited: https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-github-vulnerability Simon Willison, the lethal trifecta: https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/
